title: reAR: Rethinking Visual Autoregressive Models via Token-wise Consistency Regularization
claim: Mismatch between generated and tokenizer-friendly sequences is the hidden bottleneck; fixing it with regularization yields clear gains over prior approaches.
layout: 2 panels, left schematic then right scatter plot; captions beneath each
description: The figure has two panels. Panel (a), on the left, is a schematic of three token sequences. A purple tokenizer-friendly sequence, a red AR-generated sequence and a blue groundtruth sequence each flow through a Decoder-only Transformer. They then pass through a blue Tokenizer Codebook, an Embedding Space box and a Tokenizer Decoder, and end in cat images. Colored dots in the embedding space show the red AR-generated embedding lying away from the purple and blue manifold. The red path decodes to a visibly different cat image. Panel (b), on the right, is a bubble scatter plot of gFID (lower is better) against IS (higher is better). The bubble size shows model size. Prior methods such as AR-VQGAN, LlamaGen, VAR, RandAR and AR-WeTok are plotted, and a highlighted 'reAR-VQGAN (Ours)' sits at the favorable corner. Captions below each panel explain exposure bias and embedding unawareness.
caption: Generator-tokenizer inconsistency is the bottleneck in the visual autoregressive model.
abstract: Visual autoregressive (AR) generation offers a promising path toward unifying vision and language models, yet its performance remains suboptimal against diffusion models. Prior work often attributes this gap to tokenizer limitations and rasterization ordering. In this work, we identify a core bottleneck from the perspective of generator-tokenizer inconsistency, i.e., the AR-generated tokens may not be well-decoded by the tokenizer. To address this, we propose reAR, a simple training strategy introducing a token-wise regularization objective: when predicting the next token, the causal transformer is also trained to recover the visual embedding of the current token and predict the embedding of the target token under a noisy context. It requires no changes to the tokenizer, generation order, inference pipeline, or external models. Despite its simplicity, reAR substantially improves performance. On ImageNet, it reduces gFID from 3.02 to 1.86 and improves IS to 316.9 using a standard rasterization-based tokenizer. When applied to advanced tokenizers, it achieves a gFID of 1.42 with only 177M parameters, matching the performance with larger state-of-the-art diffusion models (675M).
